site.CAm4mgrvlaq: The Beatles made Rishikesh a world yoga name in 1968. It was a domestic Hindu pilgrimage destination long before it had any international profile; that changed in February 1968, when The Beatles travelled here for an extended meditation course at Maharishi Mahesh Yogi's ashram — the site now widely known as the Beatles Ashram, inside what is formally the Chaurasi Kutia complex. The band wrote dozens of songs during their stay, several of which appeared on the White Album, and the global attention that followed is commonly credited as the turning point that put Rishikesh on the international yoga and meditation map. The town has built on that ever since, with a large concentration of yoga ashrams, teacher-training schools, and an annual International Yoga Festival.

site.KsYfQVVRcVD: Rishikesh is a pilgrimage town because of where it sits: where the Ganga leaves the Himalayan foothills and meets the plains, a geography that has made it a natural pilgrimage point for centuries. Devotional tradition connects the name itself to Lord Vishnu — "Hrishikesh" — said to have appeared here to a sage after long austerities, and older accounts also refer to the area as "Kubjamrak." The Mahabharata and Ramayana both mention the region, and the Raghunath Temple, with its Rishikund tank, is tied to legends of Rama himself. Adi Shankaracharya's visit in the 9th century CE is often credited with lifting Rishikesh's standing as a pilgrimage centre, cementing its role as a starting point for the Char Dham routes into the mountains. For a visitor's overview, see <0>Uttarakhand Tourism's Rishikesh page</0>.

site.TQCf31yDHB6: The road from Rishikesh to Kedarnath's roadhead runs through Devprayag, Srinagar (Garhwal), Rudraprayag, and Guptakashi to Sonprayag — roughly 120-125 km, commonly a 5-6 hour drive depending on traffic and road conditions. From Sonprayag, it's about 5 km (often shuttle-only) to Gaurikund, the actual trailhead. The temple itself is reached by a 16 km trek from Gaurikund, typically taking 6-8 hours one way for an average walker, longer with rest breaks and altitude. Pony, mule, and palki (palanquin) services operate along this trail, and helicopter services fly from nearby heliports (Phata, Guptakashi, Sersi) for those who prefer not to trek — services and fares change year to year, so confirm current options before you travel.
